title: Yarn fibre types
subtitle: What the main yarn fibres are, how they behave to work with, and what they are good for
excerpt: Wool, cotton, acrylic, linen, silk, bamboo, alpaca: each fibre behaves differently on the hook and needs different care. Understanding the main groups helps you choose the right yarn for each project.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book. Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins). Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776.

glossaryTerms.definition: Yarn spun from the coats, fleece, or cocoons of animals, including wool (sheep), alpaca, mohair (goat), angora (rabbit), and silk (silkworm).
Yarn spun from plant sources, including cotton (seed pod), linen (flax stem), bamboo, and hemp.
Yarn manufactured from petroleum-based polymers, including acrylic, nylon, and polyester. Machine-washable and colourfast.

animal fibre
) or plants (
plant fibre
Synthetic fibre
is the manufactured alternative. Each type has different handling properties and care needs. Blended yarns combine two or more fibres to share their qualities.
Animal fibres

Wool: elastic and warm, with memory that helps stitches bounce back. The most forgiving fibre for beginners. Can felt if washed in hot water with agitation. Superwash wool is treated to be machine-washable.
Alpaca: softer than wool, with less elasticity. Good drape. Does not felt. Suits garments where softness against skin matters.
Mohair: very fine, with a pronounced halo that obscures stitch structure. Best on large hooks with open-stitch patterns. Hard to frog.
Silk: strong, lustrous, with no elasticity. Very slippery to work. Best in blends. Knots slip; use a Russian join for joins.
Plant fibres
Cotton: strong, machine-washable, good stitch definition. No elasticity, which means joins and edgings need more care. Heavier than wool at the same weight.
Linen: stiff when new, softens significantly with washing. Good for bags, home accessories, and kitchen items. Little elasticity.
Bamboo: smooth and slightly silky. Good drape, soft against skin. Some bamboo yarn is more akin to a semi-synthetic due to processing.
Synthetic fibres
Acrylic: machine-washable, colourfast, widely available. Does not felt. Pills with heavy wear. Sensitive to high heat.
Nylon: strong and hard-wearing. Often blended with wool in sock yarn to add durability in high-wear areas.
Blended yarns

Most commercial yarn is blended. Wool-acrylic blends are machine-washable but feel warmer than pure acrylic. Alpaca-wool blends add softness without losing the elasticity that makes a garment hold its shape. Read the ball band for the percentage breakdown: the dominant fibre determines the care requirements.
Common problems

items.symptom: The yarn label says wool but it feels scratchy and unpleasant
items.cause: Coarse wool breeds (like Shetland or Corriedale) are hardwearing but not next-to-skin soft. Fine merino is much softer.
items.fix: Check whether the label specifies the breed. For a garment that will touch skin, look for merino, BFL (Bluefaced Leicester), or alpaca blends.

items.symptom: A blended yarn melted slightly in the dryer
items.cause: The blend contained acrylic or synthetic content that is heat-sensitive.
items.fix: Check the care symbols for any blend that contains synthetic fibre before tumble drying.

content.text: What to try next

The ball band shows the fibre content as a percentage breakdown plus the care symbols derived from it. Once the main fibre types are familiar, reading a ball band takes under a minute to extract everything you need to know about care and workability.
